conflicts.meeting_title: Durham Public Schools Board of Education Monthly Meeting May 20, 2020  6:30 PM
conflicts.issue: Policy 7600 (Living Wage): Mandatory 'Shall' vs. Fiscal Hardship Safeguard ('May')
conflicts.summary: The board split across two failed votes over whether modifying Durham's longstanding living-wage policy to add a budget-shortfall exception and replace 'shall' with 'may' undermined the district's commitment to low-wage staff.
conflicts.side_a_position: Preserve the mandatory 'shall' requirement and remove all proposed financial-insufficiency exception text.
side_a_arguments: Changing 'shall' to 'may' weakens the legal commitment and singles out the lowest-paid full-time workers (custodians, bus drivers, cafeteria staff) rather than high-salaried staff.
Future boards already have authority to waive a policy in a true emergency without permanently diluting the standard.
conflicts.side_b_position: Allow a narrow fiscal-insufficiency safeguard so a future superintendent is not forced into layoffs or educational cuts during a severe downturn.
side_b_arguments: The first sentence preserves the board's living-wage commitment while the finance-officer clause handles budget-reduction mechanics realistically.

Board Attorney Rod Malone noted the draft's 'may' failed to tie non-adjustment strictly to budget cuts, prompting most proponents to vote down the draft alongside Beyer and Forte-Brown so it could be redrafted cleanly.
conflicts.resolution: After the pure-'shall' motion failed 2-5 and the administration's 'may' draft failed 1-6 (with only Matt Sears voting Aye), the board instructed Tanya Giovanni to return on June 10 with revised language restoring 'shall' and narrowing the Finance Officer advisement clause.

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham Public Schools Board of Education Monthly Meeting November 15, 2018 6:30 PM
conflicts.issue: Custodial Equipment Rebid, Prior Award Rescission, and Multi-Vendor Split
conflicts.summary: The board split 5-2 over rejecting the November 1 custodial equipment RFP award to Brame and approving a ~$727,000 line-item rebid split across Sifel Inc., Brame, and Pro-San following a vendor protest and legal counsel's clarification of contract purchase rights.
conflicts.side_a_position: Rescind the prior award and approve the line-item low-bid rebid across three vendors to ensure statutory compliance, address the vendor protest and prior contract misinterpretation, and maintain transparency on a ~$700k+ purchase.
side_a_arguments: Legal counsel advised rebidding because the original RFP scoring rubric weights and evaluation criteria were not explicitly disclosed to vendors and a formal protest was filed.

Staff corrected an erroneous interpretation of the Service Solutions contract and reduced walk-behind scrubber sizing from 28 inches to 20 inches, saving roughly $159,000 to keep the all-in cost comparable ($727,000 with taxes/fees vs. $689,000 before taxes/fees).
Going back to clarify a major contract after community and vendor scrutiny represents good governance, even while demanding stronger internal contract review going forward.
conflicts.side_b_position: Oppose rescinding the original award to Brame and splitting equipment purchases across three different vendors at essentially the same total price.
side_b_arguments: Splitting equipment across three vendors (Sifel, Brame, and Pro-San) complicates training, warranties, and maintenance compared to working with a single Durham-based vendor (Brame).

Rebidding delayed implementation ahead of the December 1 in-house transition and spent extra staff and legal time only to arrive at roughly the same price, seemingly driven by fear over a protest rather than substance.
conflicts.resolution: Motion moved by Matt Sears to reject the previous bid, rescind the prior award, and approve the new multi-vendor rebid passed 5-2 by voice/hand vote (without a read roll call).

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham Board of Education Monthly Meeting November 21, 2019 6:30 PM
conflicts.issue: Githens/Brogden Middle School Boundary West of US 15-501: NC 751 Scenario 1 vs. Cornwallis Road
conflicts.summary: Board members split 4-3 over whether to adopt staff's recommended Cornwallis Road corridor as the southern boundary between Githens and Brogden middle schools or adopt Scenario 1 (NC 751), keeping the Duke Forest/Colony Park pocket in Githens.
conflicts.side_a_position: Adopt Scenario 1 using NC 751 and Duke Forest as the boundary to keep an isolated handful of Forest View/Colony Park students with their neighborhood and elementary cohort.
side_a_arguments: Steve Unruhe argued Scenario 1 only affects a handful of students (~14 across six grades), makes virtually no capacity or operational difference, and keeps the Lemor/Colony Park pocket connected to its surrounding neighborhood.

Matt Sears supported Scenario 1 as consistent with keeping communities connected, and Xavier Cason clarified at 01:54:10 that Duke Forest functions as an undeveloped research-land natural boundary rather than an arbitrary carve-out.
conflicts.side_b_position: Maintain the administration's recommended Cornwallis Road straight-line boundary to avoid setting a precedent of carving out pockets ahead of district-wide redistricting.
side_b_arguments: Dr. Mike Lee emphasized Cornwallis Road is a clean, straight natural corridor and warned against setting a precedent of etching out small residential pockets ahead of full-district redistricting in spring 2020.

Minnie Forte-Brown raised unreadiness during the vote, noting Scenario 1 was feasible rather than staff-recommended and warning that departing from staff's boundary line sets a difficult precedent for larger upcoming redistricting decisions.
conflicts.resolution: Motion adopting Scenario 1 (NC 751) for Githens/Brogden alongside the Creekside/Parkwood recommendation passed 4-3 by voice/hand vote (with one additional Aye and one additional Nay between Natalie Beyer and Bettina Umstead not individually recorded by roll call).

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham Public Schools Board of Education Monthly Meeting May 20, 2020  6:30 PM
conflicts.issue: Approve Policy 7600 (Living Wage) as Recommended by Administration ('May' + Hardship Clause)
conflicts.summary: After the prior motion failed, a member moved and another seconded adopting administration's draft changing 'shall' to 'may' with the financial-insufficiency clause. Board Attorney Rod Malone advised that 'may' gave the superintendent broad discretion rather than limiting non-adjustment strictly to budget reductions, leading Steve Unruhe and five others to vote No so staff could rewrite the text; failed 1-6.
conflicts.side_a_position: Voted Aye (Failed 1-6)
conflicts.side_b_position: Voted Nay / Opposed
conflicts.resolution: Failed (1-6)

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham Board of Education Monthly Meeting April 23, 2020  6:30 PM
conflicts.issue: Policy 7300 Employee Recording Restrictions (Second Reading)
conflicts.summary: While six board members accepted legal counsel's reordered Policy 7300 language regulating employee recordings on school property, Matt Sears dissented in a 6-1 vote.
conflicts.side_a_position: Adopt revised Policy 7300 prohibiting secret one-party employee recordings while clarifying exceptions for approved curriculum and official business.
side_a_arguments: Reordering the clauses removes the chilling opening language identified at the April 9 work session.
Explicitly protects teachers and staff making approved instructional recordings.
conflicts.side_b_position: Oppose adopting Policy 7300 as drafted.
side_b_arguments: Recorded a dissenting vote against the policy on second reading.
conflicts.resolution: Policy 7300 passed 6-1 on second reading with Matt Sears dissenting.

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham Public Schools Board of Education Work Session   June 10, 2020  5:00 PM
conflicts.issue: Policy 3460: Lowering Graduation Credit Requirements (28 to 26) and Waiving Second Reading
conflicts.summary: Natalie Beyer initially raised concern that reducing graduation credits from 28 to 26 and waiving a second reading sent the wrong signal and bypassed teacher feedback, while a board majority urged immediate adoption to remove barriers for struggling freshmen.
conflicts.side_a_position: Hold Policy 3460 for a second reading at the monthly board meeting and examine 22-credit diploma data and teacher feedback.
side_a_arguments: Students on block schedules can earn 32 credits, so dropping to 26 without strong accelerated messaging risks signaling lowered expectations and allowing freshmen to fail three classes and advance.
The proposal appeared brand new without educator input.
conflicts.side_b_position: Waive second reading and adopt the 26-credit minimum immediately for 2020-21.
side_b_arguments: Twenty-six credits aligns with top-performing Chapel Hill (22) and Wake County, satisfies UNC system, Durham Tech, and military eligibility, and prevents struggling ninth-graders from giving up.
Early adoption lets counselors advise rising high schoolers over the summer.
conflicts.resolution: After clarifying DSA and School for Creative Studies remained at 24 credits and framing 26 as a minimum requirement, Beyer joined the unanimous 7-0 vote to waive second reading and adopt Policy 3460.

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham Public Schools Board of Education Monthly Meeting May 20, 2020  6:30 PM

conflicts.summary: A member moved and another seconded approving Policy 7600 without administration's red-text financial-exigency paragraph and with 'shall' restored. After Xavier Cason argued the revision preserved the policy's aspiration while protecting against layoffs, the motion failed 2-5.
conflicts.side_a_position: Voted Aye (Failed 2-5)
conflicts.side_b_position: Voted Nay / Opposed
conflicts.resolution: Failed (2-5)

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham Joint Board of County Commissioners and Board of Education Quarterly Meeting
conflicts.issue: FY21 County Budget Gap for DPS ($5.23M vs. $19M Request), Fund Balance Comparisons, and 2020 School Bond
conflicts.summary: DPS board members pressed county officials over the ~$15 million operating shortfall leaving $15/hour staff pay unfunded and resisted county comparisons of fund balances, while a proposal for a November 2020 bond drew county pushback.
conflicts.side_a_position: Seek deeper county operating/capital support—including exploring a modest November 2020 bond—and clarify that DPS's ~$8.3M-$11M fund balance is not comparable to the county's $62.5M unassigned ($211.1M total) reserves.
side_a_arguments: DPS's unanimous $19M request included $15/hour minimum wages for lowest-paid staff and level-funding needs (~$7M just to stay level), leaving a $15M gap.
Waiting until 2022 delays shovel-ready school projects, and DPS's small fund balance is already strained by COVID-19 expenses without net savings.
conflicts.side_b_position: Hold the FY21 increase at $5.23M ($3.2M operating, $2M capital) plus $176M in front-loaded LOBs while deferring any GO bond referendum to 2022.
side_b_arguments: A November 2020 bond would trigger an immediate property tax hike during a severe pandemic downturn, while LOBs already fund Northern High School and Elementary C.
The county carries $26M/year in existing school debt service and must preserve reserves to protect its AAA bond rating amid plunging sales taxes.
conflicts.resolution: No formal vote was taken; county staff provided the FY19 unassigned fund balance figure ($62,456,569) while both boards acknowledged continuing budget uncertainty from the General Assembly.

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham Joint Board of County Commissioners and Board of Education Quarterly Meeting
conflicts.issue: Urgency of Joint City-County-DPS CARES Act Digital Equity Plan vs. Immediate Device Ordering
conflicts.summary: Board members and county commissioners debated whether the city, county, and DPS could quickly convene a joint task force to coordinate CARES Act funds for hotspots and devices before the June 1 filing deadline.
conflicts.side_a_position: Rapidly convene city, county, and school finance/leadership staff to align CARES Act funding on student digital access and countywide broadband.
side_a_arguments: Providing hotspots and fiber access addresses both immediate remote learning gaps and long-term rural/low-income equity across Durham.
conflicts.side_b_position: DPS cannot delay ordering devices past June 1 to wait on intergovernmental CARES negotiations, and the county's $5.48M CARES allocation faces competing small-business, food, and housing emergencies.
side_b_arguments: Global Chromebook demand requires a 60-day lead time starting before June 1, forcing DPS to front costs from fund balance first.
Durham County received only $5.48M in CARES funds compared to $11M for DPS and $194M for Wake County.
conflicts.resolution: Both boards expressed support for ongoing digital-equity collaboration between managers and Digital Durham while DPS proceeded immediately with its May 28 device procurement.

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham Board of Education Work Session April 9, 2020  5:00 PM
conflicts.issue: Timing and Choice of K-5 Literacy Core Curriculum Adoption
conflicts.summary: Board members split over whether to immediately adopt staff's recommendation of Houghton Mifflin Harcourt Into Reading plus McGraw-Hill Wonders or defer two weeks to evaluate American Reading Company (ARC), single-vendor costs, and cultural responsiveness scorecards.
conflicts.side_a_position: Adopt Into Reading and Wonders immediately to honor teacher votes, maintain instructional momentum, and avoid ARC's ~$950,000 higher price tag.
side_a_arguments: Teachers voted under the agreed first- and second-choice process, and rejecting their choice undermines trust and accountability.
Further delay risks failing to have standardized literacy materials ready for the fall when proficiency is already under 50%.
ARC costs roughly $950,000 more, and specialists can supplement Wonders' social justice gaps.
conflicts.side_b_position: Defer the vote two weeks to review scorecards and multi-year pricing for all three curricula (including ARC and single-curriculum options) amid COVID-19 budget uncertainty.
side_b_arguments: Into Reading and Wonders are very similar basal readers while ARC tied for first-choice votes (10 each) and offers a distinct approach.
Wonders scored culturally insufficient on social justice, requiring supplemental materials.
A looming pandemic recession and potential state revenue shortfalls require scrutinizing multi-year financial commitments and single-vendor pricing.
conflicts.resolution: Board agreed by consensus at 02:56:11 to defer the decision two weeks to April 23 and requested full scorecards and cost comparisons.

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham Public Schools Board of Education Monthly Meeting   June 25, 2020  5:00 PM
conflicts.issue: Converting Informational Reopening Plan to Immediate Action Vote and High School Exclusion Under Plan B
conflicts.summary: Board members debated both the process of voting on an informational agenda item without advance notice and the substance of excluding high schoolers from in-person learning under Plan B.
conflicts.side_a_position: Express procedural and substantive unreadiness over rushed action, 100% remote high school learning, and missing health/staffing/hazard-pay resources.
side_a_arguments: Presenting an item as informational and voting on the fly deprives the public and board members of advance preparation.
Zero in-person time for high schoolers risks adolescent social-emotional harm; DPS also lacked nurses, hazard pay, and clear answers when 50% of teachers felt unsafe.
conflicts.side_b_position: Authorize administration immediately to begin operational preparations so timelines for August are not lost.
side_b_arguments: Even an imperfect starting benchmark is needed for staff to begin logistics, with modifications and price tags returning in July.
conflicts.resolution: After airing their concerns on the record, all six present members voted Aye (6-0) to give administration initial authorization to move forward while returning in July with detailed updates.

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham Board of Education Monthly Meeting April 23, 2020  6:30 PM
conflicts.issue: K-5 Literacy Core Curriculum Selection: Into Reading + ARC vs. Into Reading + Wonders
conflicts.summary: Board members debated whether to adopt the staff-recommended combination of Houghton Mifflin Harcourt Into Reading and McGraw-Hill Wonders based on combined first- and second-choice school votes, or pair Into Reading with American Reading Company (ARC) despite higher cost.
conflicts.side_a_position: Adopt Into Reading and American Reading Company (ARC) to provide two qualitatively distinct curriculum options and avoid Wonders' cultural responsiveness deficiencies.
side_a_arguments: ARC tied Into Reading in first-choice school votes and offers a qualitatively different instructional model than two similar basal readers.
McGraw-Hill Wonders was rated culturally insufficient on social justice and required supplemental purchases.
Investing in K-5 literacy is a top priority second only to universal Pre-K, even if future budget trade-offs are required.
conflicts.side_b_position: Follow the school vote matrix recommending Into Reading and Wonders, warning that ARC costs more and could squeeze funds for Pre-K or other priorities.
side_b_arguments: Teachers voted under an agreed first- and second-choice ranking process and deserve to see their combined vote honored.
ARC's higher cost could force cuts in other areas such as AIG or Pre-K if county funds are constrained.
conflicts.resolution: Xavier Cason moved to adopt Into Reading and ARC, and Minnie Forte-Brown joined the board in passing the motion 7-0 while urging county support for Pre-K.

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham Board of Education Monthly Meeting March 26, 2020  6:30 PM
conflicts.issue: FY 2020-21 County Budget Request: COVID-19 Austerity Reductions vs. Restoring $15 Minimum Wage, Teacher Supplements, and Counselors
conflicts.summary: Administration proposed trimming the FY 2020-21 local county budget ask from $17M to $14.3M by deferring the $15/hour classified minimum wage and teacher supplements due to COVID-19 revenue uncertainty, sparking strong pushback from board members who insisted on preserving those commitments and counselor ratios.
conflicts.side_a_position: Restore the $15/hour classified minimum wage, teacher salary supplements, and counselor ratio investments in the county budget request rather than preemptively cutting them.
side_a_arguments: Durham city and county employees already receive $15/hour, and DPS should not ask classified workers or teachers to settle for less.
Removing living-wage and supplement priorities at the start of budget negotiations preemptively concedes core equity commitments before county discussions even begin.
Counselor-to-student ratios and 1:1 device needs remain urgent, especially amid pandemic trauma.
conflicts.side_b_position: Present a trimmed $14.3M baseline request reflecting anticipated COVID-19 economic contractions while keeping deferred items ready to revisit before the May 15 statutory deadline.
side_b_arguments: The MOU budget request is a fluid starting point that can be revised as General Assembly and county revenue impacts become clearer.
Local businesses are shut down and county revenues are expected to contract sharply.
conflicts.resolution: Dr. Mike Lee accommodated the board consensus and the board voted 7-0 to approve an amended $19.38M request restoring the $15/hour minimum wage, teacher supplements, and counselors.

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham Board of Education Work Session February 13, 2020 5:00 PM
conflicts.issue: Immediate Universal Pre-K Sliding Scale Alignment at George Watts and Morehead Montessori vs. One-Year Transition Delay
conflicts.summary: The board split 4-1 over whether to apply the Durham Pre-K sliding tuition scale immediately in 2020-21 to George Watts and Morehead Montessori alongside all other DPS Pre-K sites, or grant staff's requested one-year delay to protect families who applied under the older DPS scale.
conflicts.side_a_position: Apply the Durham Pre-K sliding scale uniformly across all DPS Pre-K sites starting July 1, 2020 with no deferment for Watts and Morehead.
side_a_arguments: Durham Pre-K eliminates tuition up to 400% of the federal poverty level, delivering substantial savings to lower- and middle-income families who should not wait another year.
DPS must build one unified universal pre-K system across Durham rather than keeping two scales.
conflicts.side_b_position: Defer implementing the new scale at Watts and Morehead until 2021-22 (or allow families the lesser of the two scales) to honor prior magnet-fair marketing.
side_b_arguments: Families applied to Watts and Morehead in the fall magnet window relying on the published DPS sliding scale, and higher-income families above 400% FPL would face unexpected fee increases.
Consistency and trust require honoring commitments communicated to magnet applicants until the next application cycle.
conflicts.resolution: Minnie Forte-Brown's motion for blanket alignment without a Watts/Morehead deferment passed 4-1, with Bettina Umstead voting Nay and requesting future governance-committee scale changes still appear on DPS agendas for information.

conflicts.meeting_title: Joint Board of Education and Board of County Commissioners Quarterly Meeting  November 12, 2019 9:00
conflicts.issue: Capital Spending Pace, 2020 vs. 2022 Bond Timing, and Funding Commitments for Northern HS, Elementary C, and Elementary F
conflicts.summary: School board members and county officials/commissioners clashed over why 2016 Northern High School bond funds remained unspent, whether DPS could absorb $400 million in short-term capital spending without jeopardizing Durham County's AAA bond rating, and how to balance Elementary School F and deferred school maintenance against county CIP priorities.
conflicts.side_a_position: DPS needs an explicit county funding commitment to replenish Northern High School (via LOBs) before spending 2016 bond money on Elementary School C, plus urgent action on Elementary School F and deferred maintenance.
side_a_arguments: Dr. Mike Lee and Steve Unruhe explained DPS had held the $51 million in 2016 bonds because touching Northern High School funds without a formal county replacement commitment would alarm Northern families.

Bettina Umstead and Minnie Forte-Brown urged the county to bring prioritized CIP trade-offs to the January meeting and act on critical red/yellow facility needs rather than delaying construction while costs escalate.
conflicts.side_b_position: Durham County must preserve AAA credit metrics, manage per-capita CIP load ($1.36B), align the next GO bond to 2022, and constrain near-term spending to realistic project-management capacity.
side_b_arguments: County financial advisor Doug Carter and Budget Director Keith Lane noted DPS averaged $19–20 million/year historically (taking 11 years to spend $195 million from 2007) and warned rating agencies would scrutinize a proposed $254 million single-year peak.

County staff and BOCC Chair Wendy Jacobs emphasized all county departments, EMS, libraries, and youth detention compete from the same funding pot and urged DPS to submit prioritized needs ahead of a 2022 bond referendum.
conflicts.resolution: Resolved by informal joint consensus (declining a formal floor vote on Steve Unruhe's motion) to proceed with Elementary School C using 2016 bond funds, replenish Northern High School via LOBs and the CIP, and revisit Elementary School F and broader CIP prioritization at the January work session.

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham Public Schools Board of Education Work Session April 11, 2019 4:30 PM
conflicts.issue: Bell Schedule Change and Ending Extended Day at Y.E. Smith and C.C. Spaulding Elementary Schools
conflicts.summary: Board members divided 5-1 on a staff-requested change moving Y.E. Smith and C.C. Spaulding Elementary Schools to an 8:30 a.m. start time and ending their extended school day, debating whether halting extended-day turnaround programming and granting two schools an 8:30 a.m. start set an inequitable districtwide precedent.
conflicts.side_a_position: Approve the 8:30 a.m. bell schedule change in deference to strong school staff support while retaining after-school intervention options.
side_a_arguments: School faculty overwhelmingly backed the change (99% at Y.E. Smith and 77% at C.C. Spaulding) and principals committed to keeping after-school tutoring and enrichment.
Transportation confirmed the 8:30 a.m. schedule fits existing bus tiers without harming fleet efficiency, and extended day had not demonstrated the intended academic gains.
conflicts.side_b_position: Question ending extended-day turnaround programming before full evaluation and oppose setting a precedent of individual schools choosing 8:30 a.m. start times.
side_b_arguments: Shortening the instructional day walks back a deliberate turnaround strategy for struggling schools without clear long-term evaluation.
Because bus tiering forced many elementary schools into much earlier start times during the systemwide bell-time flip, granting two schools 8:30 a.m. starts raises fairness and precedent concerns.
conflicts.resolution: Passed 5-1 on a voice vote with one board member absent and the lone Nay voter unnamed in the audio record (Steve Unruhe moved, Bettina Umstead seconded; Natalie Beyer raised evaluation/equity questions and Dr. Mike Lee cautioned against setting a school-chosen start-time precedent while stating the board would not delay the request).

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham Public Schools Board of Education Work Session   June 10, 2020  5:00 PM
conflicts.issue: Canvas LMS Transition Concerns vs. Teacher Tools (Google Classroom / Seesaw)
conflicts.summary: Board members relayed educator anxiety over transitioning to Canvas LMS and questioned vendor assurances before testing by DPS teachers.
conflicts.side_a_position: Ensure teachers do not lose existing Google Classroom, Seesaw, or Edmodo content and verify vendor integration claims with tech-savvy DPS teachers.
side_a_arguments: DAE members and teachers reported confusion after professional development and felt tools like Seesaw are more approachable for younger learners.
Vendors often overpromise seamless integration compared to classroom reality.
conflicts.side_b_position: Standardize on Canvas LMS as a unified hub compatible with PowerSchool grade sync while keeping Google Classroom/Seesaw usable inside it.
side_b_arguments: Standardization ends family confusion across multiple platforms and saves teachers duplicate grade entry between LMS and PowerSchool.
conflicts.resolution: Staff pledged clear teacher communication and hands-on Google/Canvas troubleshooting ahead of August professional development.

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham Board of Education Work Session March 12, 2020  5:00 PM
conflicts.issue: Parent Note Requirements and Attendance/Exam Policy Waivers During COVID-19 (Policy 3410 6-1 Vote)
conflicts.summary: Board members debated whether requiring parent notes to excuse COVID-related student absences imposed an unnecessary burden during a pandemic, and voted 6-1 to waive Policy 3410's attendance requirement for high school exam exemptions.
conflicts.side_a_position: Eliminate note hurdles and trust families during the pandemic while waiving exam exemption attendance penalties.
side_a_arguments: Requiring parent notes during a global crisis creates unnecessary administrative and family burdens.
Families should be encouraged to keep at-risk children and household members home without truancy letters or exam penalties.
conflicts.side_b_position: Maintain some form of parent notification (including electronic communication) so data managers can code lawful absences under DPI rules.
side_b_arguments: State DPI attendance statutes govern lawful versus unlawful absence coding.
Schools still need parent notification to account for student whereabouts.
conflicts.resolution: Staff confirmed automated truancy/DA letters would not trigger and electronic notes were acceptable; the board passed the Policy 3410 exam exemption waiver 6-1 (lone dissenter not named in audio).

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham Board of Education Work Session March 12, 2020  5:00 PM
conflicts.issue: Immediate School Closure vs. Phased Operational Preparation
conflicts.summary: Board members disagreed sharply over whether DPS should close schools immediately on Monday, March 16 for public health protection or take several days to finalize meal distribution, instructional packets, and classified employee pay logistics.
conflicts.side_a_position: Close DPS schools immediately on Monday, March 16 to flatten the curve and protect students, families, and hourly staff.
side_a_arguments: Durham County had severe testing shortages (reportedly only three tests received), meaning community spread was likely already underway.
Proactive school closures ahead of the epidemic curve provide public health protection, whereas reactive closures do not.
Classified staff and families should not remain exposed while neighboring districts like Chapel Hill-Carrboro and Orange were closing.
conflicts.side_b_position: Take 2–3 days to prepare instructional packets, meal distribution, and state legislative guidance on hourly employee pay before closing.
side_b_arguments: Unlike 1:1 districts, DPS lacked devices and internet access for many of its 34,000 students and needed print packets.
Closing without legislative action left hourly classified employees with exhausted leave unpaid and halted school-based breakfast/lunch access.
conflicts.resolution: At 02:22:17, Superintendent Dr. Pascal Mubenga announced DPS would close schools effective Monday, March 16 with detailed guidance issued the next day, and the board voted 7-0 to grant him emergency policy-waiver authority.

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham Board of Education Work Session January 9, 2020 5:00 PM
conflicts.issue: Approach to Charter School Local Authorization Pilot and Legislative Outreach
conflicts.summary: Board members disagreed on whether to pursue a formal letter to state education/legislative officials regarding charter school authorization and racial isolation versus focusing strictly on a neutral-facilitated local conversation with Durham's 14 brick-and-mortar charter schools first.
conflicts.side_a_position: Initiate a local-bill authorization pilot conversation and write to the State Board of Education addressing racial isolation and segregation concerns.
side_a_arguments: 90% of charter school authorizers nationwide are local education agencies (LEAs), and local school board governance improves transparency, equity, and accountability.
The NC Charter Advisory Board recently removed language on racial isolation and segregation from its report, warranting a board letter to the State Board.
A local bill in the General Assembly could proceed if even one or two Durham charter schools are interested.
conflicts.side_b_position: Avoid sending an uncoordinated letter to Raleigh or leading with legislation; instead, have a neutral third party convene an initial local listening conversation with Durham charter schools.
side_b_arguments: Sending a broadcast letter to Raleigh without charter school board co-signers or prior organizing would likely be ignored (Dr. Mike Lee).

A legislative bill is far down the road, and charter schools will not engage meaningfully if DPS appears to dictate terms rather than joining a neutral table convened by the DPS Foundation or a university (Steve Unruhe).

Matt Sears questioned the timing and lack of prior charter interest, while Superintendent Dr. Pascal Mubenga cautioned against conversations turning into requests for DPS operational/transportation subsidies without board accountability.
conflicts.resolution: No formal vote was taken; by consensus, the board directed administration to explore a neutral facilitating organization to invite Durham's 14 brick-and-mortar charter schools to an initial local conversation.

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham Board of Education Work Session April 9, 2020  5:00 PM
conflicts.issue: Policy 7300 Prohibition on One-Party Employee Recordings
conflicts.summary: Board members challenged proposed Policy 7300 language barring one-party employee recordings on school property without principal/supervisor permission as overly broad and potentially chilling official-business recordings.
conflicts.side_a_position: Prohibit secret one-party recordings to ensure staff and coworkers feel safe from unfair covert recording.
side_a_arguments: Secret recordings can chill candid workplace conversations among supervisors and staff.
conflicts.side_b_position: Narrow the prohibition to secret recordings and explicitly protect official-business and instructional recordings.
side_b_arguments: Barring recordings without supervisor/principal permission is too restrictive and does not clearly protect official business.
conflicts.resolution: Board voted 7-0 to advance the other 7000A policies to consent while returning Policy 7300 with revised wording at the April 23 meeting.

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham Board of Education Work Session June 6, 2019 4:30
conflicts.issue: School-level opt-outs vs. universal implementation of K-5 Eureka Math curriculum
conflicts.summary: Following public comment from Club Boulevard Elementary parents requesting an opt-out or slower transition from Bridges Math, board members differed over whether to formalize school-level implementation flexibility or enforce uniform district-wide adoption to close racial achievement gaps. Ultimately, the board approved the Great Minds Eureka Math contract unanimously (5-0) while leaving school-level pacing as an administrative responsibility rather than adopting a board policy opt-out.
conflicts.side_a_position: Support gradual, differentiated rollout flexibility for schools with existing math curricula
side_a_arguments: Respect the professional judgment and prior investments of principals and teachers at schools already using vetted curricula like Bridges Math
Provide differentiated professional development and avoid overwhelming teachers and families with rapid simultaneous math and ELA changes
Treat school-level implementation pacing as tactical administrative discretion rather than a rigid top-down mandate
conflicts.side_b_position: Oppose formal school opt-outs or citywide flexibility that leaves vulnerable students behind
side_b_arguments: All 30 elementary schools participated in the vote (19-11 for Eureka Math), making the selection participatory rather than top-down

Stark 3rd-grade math proficiency gaps persist (48.6% for Black males and 49.8% for Black females vs. ~85% for white students), and mobile low-income students suffer when transferring between schools with mismatched curricula
A slower rollout is acceptable only if every school commits to implementing Eureka Math rather than opting out
conflicts.resolution: Great Minds Eureka Math contract passed 5-0 without a separate board motion authorizing opt-outs, with staff committing to work with principals on transition pacing and report back in October.

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham Board of Education Work Session December 6, 2018 4;30 PM
conflicts.issue: Cancellation of December 20, 2018 Board Meeting
conflicts.summary: The board voted 5-1 to cancel the December 20, 2018 regular monthly meeting after discussing potential impacts on pre-January 4 personnel hires and irregular January–June 2019 meeting dates.
conflicts.side_a_position: Cancel the December 20, 2018 meeting since no work-session items required action and handle any urgent January hires via phone closed session if needed.
side_a_arguments: No action items were advancing from the work session to the December 20 meeting, matching the prior two years' practice of canceling late-December meetings.
Urgent personnel reports before the January 4 teacher workday could be reviewed and acted upon by phone if required, while 2019 calendar dates could be reviewed in January.
conflicts.side_b_position: Retain the scheduled December 20 meeting (one dissenting vote recorded without roll-call identification).
side_b_arguments: Leaving a gap until January 10 is a long interval for personnel actions and other district business before the new semester.
conflicts.resolution: Motion to cancel the December 20, 2018 meeting passed 5-1; specific votes of the other four members present besides mover Steve Unruhe and seconder Minnie Forte-Brown were not named in a roll call.

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham Board of Education Monthly Meeting January 23 , 2020 6:30 PM
conflicts.issue: 2016 Bond Funding Allocation for School Security Vestibules
conflicts.summary: During approval of the $3.72 million 2016 bond transfer, a board member criticized spending ~$3 million on security vestibules as driven by fear rather than data, while Chair Dr. Mike Lee defended vestibules as strongly supported by staff, parents, and students.
conflicts.side_a_position: Question allocating roughly $3 million of 2016 bond funds to security vestibules as an over-reaction not grounded in data.
side_a_arguments: Security vestibule spending and active-shooter insurance represent an over-response driven by fear rather than data analysis.
Future capital spending decisions should rely on stronger data analysis.
conflicts.side_b_position: Support completing security vestibule projects as a practical safety enhancement welcomed by school communities.
side_b_arguments: Overwhelmingly, staff, parents, and older students at schools like Rogers-Herr express appreciation for secure front-office entry vestibules.
Vestibules do not disrupt the daily flow of school while providing valuable safety protection.
conflicts.resolution: Despite the recorded policy disagreement, the board approved the full $3,719,538 2016 bond fund transfer 7-0.

conflicts.issue: Adoption of Fall 2020 Student Reassignment Plan (Creekside/Parkwood & Githens/Brogden Scenario 1 along NC 751)
conflicts.summary: Adopted the administration's Creekside Elementary-to-Parkwood Elementary reassignment recommendation and modified the Githens/Brogden Middle School recommendation west of US 15-501 to Scenario 1 (NC 751 boundary) instead of Cornwallis Road.
conflicts.side_a_position: Voted Aye (Passed 4-3)
conflicts.side_b_position: Voted Nay / Opposed
conflicts.resolution: Passed (4-3)

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham Public Schools Board of Education Monthly Meeting March 21
conflicts.issue: Take Two Summer EOG/EOC Retesting Authorization ($250,000 Earmarked State/Federal Funds)
conflicts.summary: The board split 5-1 on authorizing Take Two summer EOG/EOC retesting (~$250,000, limited to ELA and science in 2019 because state math tests were being renormed), contrasting skepticism of high-stakes standardized testing with arguments for student proficiency opportunities and future exam readiness.
conflicts.side_a_position: Approve Take Two summer retesting using earmarked state and federal funds and comply with annual NCDPI authorization requirements.
side_a_arguments: Earmarked state and federal funds were budgeted specifically for retesting and cannot simply be diverted outside testing requirements.
Retesting builds student confidence and prepares students for future gatekeeper standardized exams such as the ACT, LSAT, MCAT, and bar exam.
conflicts.side_b_position: Oppose spending $250,000 on additional high-stakes 'bubble tests' when North Carolina promotion decisions do not require retesting.
side_b_arguments: High-stakes standardized 'bubble testing' creates misplaced incentives to boost scores rather than investing the $250,000 in more meaningful summer instruction.
Principals retain promotion discretion under state law without relying on summer retests.
conflicts.resolution: Motion passed 5-1 by voice vote with Matt Sears confirmed absent; the audio transcript did not state the individual names of the five Aye voters or the lone Nay voter among the six seated members present (Dr. Mike Lee, Bettina Umstead, Natalie Beyer, Minnie Forte-Brown, Xavier Cason, and Steve Unruhe).

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham Public Schools Board of Education Work Session February 7, 2019 4:30 PM
conflicts.issue: Aligning 2019-20 Traditional and Year-Round Spring Breaks Over Year-Round School Preferences
conflicts.summary: Following the board's January 24 referral of spring break dates back to schools, members clashed over whether to enforce a single districtwide spring break (Draft B) or honor the 4-1 (80%) vote by year-round schools to retain Draft A.
conflicts.side_a_position: Align traditional and year-round spring break weeks districtwide to simplify scheduling for multi-school families.
side_a_arguments: 61% of all voting DPS schools preferred having a single common spring break across traditional and year-round calendars, and 73% of overall school votes backed Draft B.
Families with children attending both traditional and year-round campuses face childcare and vacation disruptions when spring breaks fall in different weeks.
conflicts.side_b_position: Respect the 80% (4-1) vote of year-round schools favoring Draft A and avoid forcing Draft B's mid-quarter disruption onto year-round calendars.
side_b_arguments: Four of five year-round schools repeatedly voted for Draft A because Draft B cuts two weeks into their third-quarter instructional cycle right before intercession.
Overriding a 4-1 campus majority among year-round schools contradicts the district's collaborative calendar-voting process.
conflicts.resolution: When Chair Dr. Mike Lee called at 01:31:51 for any motion to reconsider or modify the calendars previously adopted on January 10, no board member made a motion, leaving Traditional Draft B and Year-Round Draft A unchanged.

conflicts.summary: Following a one-hour closed session, the board approved an amendment to Paragraph 12 of Superintendent Dr. Pascal Mubenga's contract by a 4-1 vote.
conflicts.side_a_position: Approve the closed-session amendment to Paragraph 12 of the superintendent's contract.
side_a_arguments: Discussed and negotiated during closed session prior to the open-session vote.
conflicts.side_b_position: Oppose the contract amendment (one Nay vote cast).

conflicts.side_a_position: Approve the superintendent's October 18, 2018 personnel report recommendations.

conflicts.side_b_position: Oppose approval of the personnel report (one Nay vote cast).

conflicts.resolution: Motion passed 5-1 by voice/hand vote without a read roll call naming the five Aye voters or the single Nay voter.

meetings.title: Durham Public Schools Board of Education Monthly Meeting   June 25, 2020  5:00 PM
meetings.executive_summary: At its June 25, 2020 monthly meeting presided over by Chair Dr. Mike Lee—the final meeting of outgoing board members Minnie Forte-Brown and Steve Unruhe—the Durham Public Schools Board of Education celebrated the Durham Feast meal program, a 400-Chromebook Lenovo donation, and Governor's School honorees, and voted 6-0 (with Forte-Brown recused) to rename the DPS Staff Development Center the Minnie M. Forte-Brown Center for Staff Development after Forte-Brown's 16 years on the board. After reporting 395 public comments (320 calling for removal of school resource officers) and unanimously passing its four-item consent agenda 7-0, the board reviewed facility rental management plans (Facilitron) and a three-plan (A/B/C) fall reopening framework featuring pre-K-8/EC/ESL in-person and high school 100% remote under Plan B. Despite objections from Natalie Beyer and Xavier Cason over converting an informational item into an action vote without prior public notice and concerns from Matt Sears and Beyer over high school isolation and insufficient nurse/hazard-pay resources, the board voted 6-0 (with Forte-Brown temporarily absent at a graduation) to authorize administration to proceed with Plan B/reopening preparations, and also approved 6-0 joining the City-County Community Safety and Wellness Task Force, the May 20 minutes, and the June 25 personnel report.

agenda_items.title: Celebrations, Lenovo Chromebook Donation, and Farewell Tribute to Minnie Forte-Brown and Steve Unruhe
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Chip Sudderth and DPS Foundation Executive Director Megan Gonzales-Smith highlighted the Durham Feast summer feeding program and Accelerating Digital Equity campaign, Lenovo announced a 400-Chromebook donation, and 25 Governor's School honorees were recognized. Board members then honored outgoing members Steve Unruhe (4 years on the board, 35 years in DPS) and Minnie Forte-Brown (16 years on the board, 4 years as Chair), voting 6-0 on a motion by Unruhe to name the Staff Development Center the Minnie M. Forte-Brown Center for Staff Development.

agenda_items.title: Agenda Approval, General Public Comment, and Outgoing Member Farewell Remarks
agenda_items.discussion_summary: The board approved its agenda 7-0 as amended to add the City-County Community Safety and Wellness Task Force. Chip Sudderth reported 395 public comments—75 addressing remote learning and technology (including Parents of African American Children) and 320 demanding removal of School Resource Officers (SROs)—before Minnie Forte-Brown and Steve Unruhe delivered emotional farewell addresses.

agenda_items.title: Consent Agenda Approval
agenda_items.discussion_summary: On a motion by Steve Unruhe and second by Minnie Forte-Brown, the board unanimously approved the four-item consent agenda 7-0: Alternative School Accountability Model, Visually Impaired Contract, CTE Local Plan, and FY 2019-20 Budget Amendment #2.

agenda_items.title: Operational Services: Facility Rental Management and Facilitron Transition
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Dr. Julius Monk and Dr. Anderson reported that facility rental revenues fell from $489,000 in 2011 to $179,000 in 2018 while policies/rates remained unchanged since 2007 and over $1 million in fees were waived against in-kind donations across ~11,900 annual events. Staff outlined adopting Facilitron online rental software (funded by a $25-$35 customer transaction fee) in Step 1 ahead of a September 2020 rate and policy proposal.

agenda_items.title: COVID-19 Reopening Task Force Update and Plan B Authorization
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Public health nurse Susan Thompson reported 3,476 Durham COVID-19 cases (631 active) with youth under 18 rising from 9% to 16% of cases, and Dr. Hardy and Dr. Monk outlined Plans A, B, and C—proposing under Plan B to serve Pre-K-8, ESL, and EC students in person in 10-15 student classrooms while keeping high schoolers 100% remote due to bus capacity (24 students/bus with masks, 8 without). After debating high school social-emotional impacts, nurse/cleaning shortages, and moving an informational item to action, the board voted 6-0 (Forte-Brown absent) to convert the item to action and authorize administration to proceed with the plan.

agenda_items.title: Community Safety and Wellness Task Force Bylaws Approval
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Bettina Umstead reported discussions with Mayor Pro Tem Jillian Johnson to add five school board representatives to the joint City-County Community Safety and Wellness Task Force and add the DPS Board Chair alongside the Mayor and BOCC Chair in selecting co-chairs. The board approved participating in the task force with those bylaws amendments 6-0 (Forte-Brown absent).

agenda_items.title: Closed Session, May 20 Minutes, and June 25 Personnel Report
agenda_items.discussion_summary: After reading a four-year board accomplishments summary, the board entered closed session 6-0. Returning at 03:57:10, the six remaining members unanimously approved the May 20, 2020 meeting minutes 6-0 and the June 25, 2020 personnel report 6-0 before adjourning.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Closed session, May 20 minutes, and Personnel report each passed 6-0

votes.item_title: Rename Staff Development Center the Minnie M. Forte-Brown Center for Staff Development
votes.notes: Minnie Forte-Brown was the honoree and did not vote on the motion.
votes.discussion_detail: Steve Unruhe moved (seconded collectively by board members) instructing administration to tentatively name the DPS Staff Development Center the Minnie M. Forte-Brown Center for Staff Development in honor of Forte-Brown's 16 years of board service, with an unveiling ceremony to follow. Passed 6-0.

votes.item_title: Approval of June 25, 2020 Monthly Meeting Agenda as Amended
votes.discussion_detail: Xavier Cason moved and another member seconded approving the agenda as amended to add the Community Safety and Wellness Task Force item. Passed 7-0.

votes.item_title: Convert Reopening Plan to Action Item and Authorize Administration to Proceed
votes.notes: Minnie Forte-Brown stepped away temporarily to attend a graduation.
votes.discussion_detail: Steve Unruhe moved and Xavier Cason seconded moving the COVID-19 reopening plan from information to action and authorizing administration to proceed with operational preparations while bringing back updated costs and community-partner details in July. Passed 6-0.

votes.item_title: Approve Participation in Joint Community Safety and Wellness Task Force with Bylaws Changes
votes.discussion_detail: Bettina Umstead moved (seconded by another member) approving DPS participation in the Community Safety and Wellness Task Force with bylaws amendments ensuring five board representatives and DPS Chair participation in co-chair selection. Passed 6-0.

votes.item_title: Motion to Enter Closed Session
votes.discussion_detail: Steve Unruhe moved and Bettina Umstead seconded entering closed session. Passed 6-0.

votes.discussion_detail: Returning to open session, a board member moved and another seconded approving the May 20, 2020 meeting minutes. Passed 6-0.

votes.discussion_detail: Matt Sears moved and Steve Unruhe seconded approving the June 25, 2020 personnel report as discussed in closed session. Passed 6-0.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham Public Schools Board of Education Monthly Meeting   June 25, 2020  5:00 PM
disagreements.issue: Converting Informational Reopening Plan to Immediate Action Vote and High School Exclusion Under Plan B
disagreements.summary: Board members debated both the process of voting on an informational agenda item without advance notice and the substance of excluding high schoolers from in-person learning under Plan B.
disagreements.side_a_position: Express procedural and substantive unreadiness over rushed action, 100% remote high school learning, and missing health/staffing/hazard-pay resources.
side_a_arguments: Presenting an item as informational and voting on the fly deprives the public and board members of advance preparation.
Zero in-person time for high schoolers risks adolescent social-emotional harm; DPS also lacked nurses, hazard pay, and clear answers when 50% of teachers felt unsafe.
disagreements.side_b_position: Authorize administration immediately to begin operational preparations so timelines for August are not lost.
side_b_arguments: Even an imperfect starting benchmark is needed for staff to begin logistics, with modifications and price tags returning in July.
disagreements.resolution: After airing their concerns on the record, all six present members voted Aye (6-0) to give administration initial authorization to move forward while returning in July with detailed updates.

meetings.title: Durham Public Schools Board of Education Work Session   June 10, 2020  5:00 PM
meetings.executive_summary: At its June 10, 2020 work session—opened and closed by Chair Dr. Mike Lee with Matt Sears presiding over the Academic Services segment—Lee addressed over 2,000 community petitions calling to end the Durham County Sheriff's Office School Resource Officer (SRO) MOU, affirming trauma over police brutality while insisting a viable safety replacement must precede removal via a community forum. The board unanimously passed its amended agenda and five consent items 7-0, and resolved its May deadlock on Policy 7600 (Living Wage) by unanimously approving 7-0 revised text retaining 'shall' alongside a Finance Officer advisement clause on budget insufficiency (while Natalie Beyer lamented the county falling one vote short on $15/hour funding). Over initial unreadiness from Natalie Beyer regarding lowered expectations and waiving second reading, the board voted 7-0 to waive second reading and adopt Policy 3460 reducing minimum graduation credits from 28 to 26 (keeping DSA and School for Creative Studies at 24). The board also unanimously approved the revised 2020-21 traditional calendar, reviewed the Ignite Online Academy and Canvas LMS integration (addressing DAE/teacher concerns over Google Classroom/Seesaw compatibility), heard rising Latinx COVID-19 case data (67.4% of May cases), approved the PowerSchool online enrollment contract 7-0, reappointed Chuck Wilson to the Durham Tech Board of Trustees, approved May 7 minutes, and adopted the June 10 personnel report 7-0.

agenda_items.title: Opening Remarks on SRO MOU, Agenda Approval, and Superintendent Recognition
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Chair Dr. Mike Lee responded to calls to discontinue the Sheriff's Office SRO MOU, describing his personal experience with police stops while stating that SRO roles had been curtailed and could only be removed once a viable safety replacement is identified at a community forum. The board approved its agenda 7-0 (adding Durham Tech Trustee reappointment), recognized Dr. Pascal Mubenga as regional Superintendent of the Year, and heard public comment summaries (including a >2,000-signature SRO letter).

agenda_items.title: Consent Agenda Approval (Items 6a-6e)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: On a motion by Dr. Mike Lee and second by Steve Unruhe, the board unanimously approved Consent Agenda Items 6a through 6e by a 7-0 roll-call vote.

agenda_items.title: Policy 7600 (Living Wage) Second Reading
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Chief of Staff Tanya Giovanni presented revised Policy 7600 restoring 'shall' for annual Durham County living-wage adjustments while requiring the Finance Officer to advise the superintendent and board if insufficient funding would compel layoffs or program cuts. Although Natalie Beyer still questioned needing the second paragraph and noted the county fell one vote short of $15/hour funding, members praised the compromise and adopted Policy 7600 7-0.

agenda_items.title: Policy 3460: Graduation Requirements Reduction from 28 to 26 Credits
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Dr. Nakia Hardy and Dr. LaVerne Mattocks-Perry recommended amending Policy 3460 to lower minimum graduation credits from 28 to 26 starting in 2020-21 (while keeping DSA and School for Creative Studies at 24 and adjusting 9th-grade promotion standards), matching neighboring districts and expanding Durham Tech/CTE access. Natalie Beyer expressed concern about messaging lowered expectations and requested waiting for second reading, while Minnie Forte-Brown, Xavier Cason, Dr. Mike Lee, and Steve Unruhe argued immediate adoption removed barriers for struggling freshmen; Beyer joined the 7-0 vote to waive second reading and adopt.

agenda_items.title: 2020-21 Traditional School Calendar Approval
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Dr. Hardy and Jamie Stroud presented the revised traditional calendar complying with state COVID-19 legislation (August 17 student start, June 11 end, five added days, five remote learning days, aligned spring break with year-round schools, and workdays on Yom Kippur and Eid). Steve Unruhe criticized the state's inflexible remote-day mandates while backing staff's plan, and the board adopted the calendar 7-0.

agenda_items.title: Ignite Online Academy and Canvas LMS Integration Discussion
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Dr. Hardy and Ms. Sidbury introduced Ignite Online Academy (K-12 virtual school taught by DPS teachers using Canvas LMS) to expand course equity, credit recovery, and pandemic options. Dr. Mike Lee, Matt Sears, and Natalie Beyer relayed DAE/teacher concerns over dropping Google Classroom or Seesaw; staff confirmed teachers could embed those tools inside Canvas with PowerSchool grade sync, while Sears urged testing by DPS teachers rather than relying on vendor claims.

agenda_items.title: COVID-19 Public Health and Reentry Task Force Update
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Public Health Nurse Susan Thompson reported Durham COVID-19 cases rose to 2,336 (17% positivity) with Hispanic residents accounting for 67.4% of May cases despite making up 14% of the population, especially in zip codes 27704, 27705, and 27707. Board members pressed for Spanish outreach, testing/tracing plans, staff childcare, and liability clarity ahead of reopening.

agenda_items.title: PowerSchool Online Enrollment Contract and Durham Tech Trustee Reappointment
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Staff presented a PowerSchool Group LLC online student enrollment contract funded from unused testing budgets, which passed 7-0 after Minnie Forte-Brown returned to cast the seventh Aye. Chair Dr. Mike Lee then presented the reappointment of Chuck Wilson to the Durham Technical Community College Board of Trustees, which passed unanimously.

agenda_items.discussion_summary: At Steve Unruhe's prompt, the board unanimously approved the May 7, 2020 work session minutes, reviewed follow-up items, and entered closed session 7-0. Returning at 03:38:54, the board unanimously approved the June 10, 2020 personnel report as amended 7-0 and adjourned.

votes.discussion_detail: Natalie Beyer moved and Bettina Umstead seconded approving the revised 2020-21 traditional school calendar complying with state COVID-19 legislation. Passed 7-0.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham Public Schools Board of Education Work Session   June 10, 2020  5:00 PM
disagreements.issue: Policy 3460: Lowering Graduation Credit Requirements (28 to 26) and Waiving Second Reading
disagreements.summary: Natalie Beyer initially raised concern that reducing graduation credits from 28 to 26 and waiving a second reading sent the wrong signal and bypassed teacher feedback, while a board majority urged immediate adoption to remove barriers for struggling freshmen.
disagreements.side_a_position: Hold Policy 3460 for a second reading at the monthly board meeting and examine 22-credit diploma data and teacher feedback.
side_a_arguments: Students on block schedules can earn 32 credits, so dropping to 26 without strong accelerated messaging risks signaling lowered expectations and allowing freshmen to fail three classes and advance.
The proposal appeared brand new without educator input.
disagreements.side_b_position: Waive second reading and adopt the 26-credit minimum immediately for 2020-21.
side_b_arguments: Twenty-six credits aligns with top-performing Chapel Hill (22) and Wake County, satisfies UNC system, Durham Tech, and military eligibility, and prevents struggling ninth-graders from giving up.
Early adoption lets counselors advise rising high schoolers over the summer.
disagreements.resolution: After clarifying DSA and School for Creative Studies remained at 24 credits and framing 26 as a minimum requirement, Beyer joined the unanimous 7-0 vote to waive second reading and adopt Policy 3460.

meetings.title: Durham Public Schools Board of Education Special Meeting May 28, 2020  5:00 PM
meetings.executive_summary: At a specially called May 28, 2020 meeting presided over by Chair Dr. Mike Lee, the Durham Public Schools Board of Education unanimously approved adding an urgent building-disinfection contract to the agenda and then acted on two pandemic-readiness procurements. Following a presentation on the one-to-one technology plan ($10.3M full package including $6.89M for 20,000 Lenovo 300e touchscreen Chromebooks, 1% hot spares, local CelTech repair support, charging carts, three-year battery and four-year accidental damage warranties, and LAN School software), Natalie Beyer questioned bundling over $2.4 million in recurring hotspot costs before Durham County and the City committed to cost-sharing; Superintendent Dr. Pascal Mubenga agreed only the devices required immediate ordering by the June 1 queue deadline, and the board voted 7-0 to approve purchasing everything presented except the hotspots (funded initially from fund balance pending CARES Act reimbursement). The board also unanimously approved 7-0 a $154,660.25 contract with Jani-King—the lowest of five bids—to clean and disinfect all schools before staff and students returned June 8 to retrieve belongings while 94% of custodial staff remained on state emergency leave.

agenda_items.title: Call to Order, Moment of Silence, and Agenda Approval
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Chair Dr. Mike Lee called the special meeting to order with a moment of silence for lives impacted by police brutality. At Dr. Julius Monk's request, the board unanimously voted 7-0 to amend the agenda by adding an urgent school cleaning and disinfecting contract after the one-to-one technology item.

agenda_items.title: One-to-One Technology Initiative: Chromebook and Cart Procurement
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Chief of Staff Tanya Giovanni, IT Director Benjamin Brown, and Dr. Pascal Mubenga presented the $10.3 million one-to-one package (20,000 Lenovo 300e touchscreen Chromebooks, carts, 1% hot spares, local CelTech warranty servicing, 1,000 adapters, white-glove provisioning, plus ~$2.4M+ for hotspots) needed by a June 1 order deadline for mid-July delivery. Addressing Xavier Cason's Zoom-compatibility questions, Natalie Beyer's equitable-distribution and 10-gig e-rate bandwidth questions, and Beyer's concern over buying hotspots prior to county cost-sharing, the board amended the motion to approve everything presented except hotspots, passing 7-0.

agenda_items.title: School Cleaning and Disinfecting Contract (Jani-King)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Dr. Julius Monk explained that with 94% of custodians remaining on state extended emergency leave (only 6% returning), schools used for meal distribution, device handoffs, and pest treatment required CDC-recommended cleaning before staff and students returned June 8 to retrieve belongings. After confirming Jani-King was significantly lower than four competing bids and asking whether the franchise was minority-owned, the board unanimously approved the $154,660.25 contract 7-0.

votes.item_title: Approval of May 28, 2020 Special Meeting Agenda as Amended
votes.discussion_detail: A board member moved and another seconded approving the agenda with the urgent cleaning and disinfecting contract added. Chair Dr. Mike Lee conducted a roll-call vote and announced unanimous passage.

votes.discussion_detail: Natalie Beyer moved (and amended to include carts) to approve procuring everything presented in the one-to-one package except the hotspots, seconded by another member, using fund balance to meet the June 1 order deadline pending CARES Act reimbursement. Passed 7-0.

votes.discussion_detail: A board member moved and another seconded approving the $154,660.25 contract with Jani-King for pre-reentry school cleaning and high-touch disinfection. Passed 7-0.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham Public Schools Board of Education Monthly Meeting May 20, 2020  6:30 PM
disagreements.issue: Policy 7600 (Living Wage): Mandatory 'Shall' vs. Fiscal Hardship Safeguard ('May')
disagreements.summary: The board split across two failed votes over whether modifying Durham's longstanding living-wage policy to add a budget-shortfall exception and replace 'shall' with 'may' undermined the district's commitment to low-wage staff.
disagreements.side_a_position: Preserve the mandatory 'shall' requirement and remove all proposed financial-insufficiency exception text.
side_a_arguments: Changing 'shall' to 'may' weakens the legal commitment and singles out the lowest-paid full-time workers (custodians, bus drivers, cafeteria staff) rather than high-salaried staff.
Future boards already have authority to waive a policy in a true emergency without permanently diluting the standard.
disagreements.side_b_position: Allow a narrow fiscal-insufficiency safeguard so a future superintendent is not forced into layoffs or educational cuts during a severe downturn.
side_b_arguments: The first sentence preserves the board's living-wage commitment while the finance-officer clause handles budget-reduction mechanics realistically.

Board Attorney Rod Malone noted the draft's 'may' failed to tie non-adjustment strictly to budget cuts, prompting most proponents to vote down the draft alongside Beyer and Forte-Brown so it could be redrafted cleanly.
disagreements.resolution: After the pure-'shall' motion failed 2-5 and the administration's 'may' draft failed 1-6 (with only Matt Sears voting Aye), the board instructed Tanya Giovanni to return on June 10 with revised language restoring 'shall' and narrowing the Finance Officer advisement clause.

meetings.title: Durham Joint Board of County Commissioners and Board of Education Quarterly Meeting
meetings.executive_summary: At the May 19, 2020 virtual quarterly joint meeting of the Durham Board of County Commissioners and Durham Public Schools Board of Education presided over by DPS Chair Dr. Mike Lee, the boards unanimously approved the agenda and reviewed the county's revised 10-year Capital Improvement Plan—which expanded school capital allocations from $320 million to $482.5 million, including $176 million in LOBs for Northern High School and Elementary School C plus planned 2022 and 2026 GO bonds. Officials discussed transitioning the Durham Feast pandemic feeding initiative into DPS's June 8 summer feeding program, DPS's 'Growing Together' student-assignment and boundary equity plan, and DPS's urgent June 1 timeline to order 1:1 student devices using fund balance pending CARES Act funding. During the FY 2020-21 county budget presentation, DPS members Natalie Beyer, Minnie Forte-Brown, and Dr. Mike Lee pressed county officials on the ~$15 million gap between DPS's $19 million request and the manager's recommended $5.23 million increase ($3.2M operations, $2M capital) and disputed fund-balance comparisons, while Beyer floated a modest November 2020 school bond that county leaders cautioned would force tax hikes amid COVID-19 revenue losses. The meeting closed with an update on a joint city-county-DPS face-covering procurement effort bolstered by $40,000 from the city and $10,000 from DPS travel savings.

agenda_items.title: Call to Order, Moment of Silence, and Joint Agenda Approval
agenda_items.discussion_summary: DPS Chair Dr. Mike Lee opened with a moment of silence honoring first responders and essential workers during COVID-19. After BOCC Vice Chair Wendy Jacobs requested time for a face-covering update and Steve Unruhe urged keeping items moving within the two-hour window, the joint boards approved the agenda unanimously by roll call.

agenda_items.title: Durham County and DPS Capital Improvement Plan (CIP) Update
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Interim/Deputy County Manager Claudia Hager and Budget Director Keith Lane reported the manager's recommended FY21 budget raised DPS 10-year CIP funding from $320M to $482.5M ($176M in LOBs for Northern High School and Elementary C, planned 2022 and 2026 GO bonds, $1M/year released lottery funds, and a $2M increase in annual current capital to $3.37M alongside ~$26M/year in school debt service). Dr. Julius Monk noted Elementary C aimed to break ground in August and Northern in late fall, and confirmed Hillside High lighting was in year-one funding.

agenda_items.title: Community Feeding Program (Durham Feast) Sustainability
agenda_items.discussion_summary: County staff (Drew Cummings and Donna Rewalt) and Dr. Julius Monk reviewed transitioning from the DPS Foundation/Food Insight Group Durham Feast partnership to DPS's traditional 24-site summer feeding program on June 8 once staff returned from emergency leave, while the Foundation continued Wednesday home deliveries to ~1,000 vulnerable families. BOCC Vice Chair Wendy Jacobs flagged that county CARES funding would be needed to sustain adult meal support.

agenda_items.title: Growing Together: Plans for Growth, Equity, and Access
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Dr. Julius Monk and School Planning Director Matthew Palmer presented DPS's 18-month 'Growing Together' student assignment, magnet, and boundary-equity framework addressing 22 of 30 elementary schools at or over capacity, ~3,000 projected students from >10,000 planned residential units, and over $500M in deferred maintenance ahead of Elementary C (2022) and F (2023). Natalie Beyer suggested a modest November 2020 bond to accelerate shovel-ready projects, which county commissioners and Claudia Hager resisted due to immediate tax impacts and LOB sequencing ahead of 2022.

agenda_items.title: DPS 1:1 Technology Plan and Joint CARES Act Coordination
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Chief of Staff Tanya Giovanni outlined DPS's $6.89M 1:1 device estimate and June 1 ordering deadline, while CFO Paul LeSieur noted DPS's ~$8.3M-$11M fund balance and June 1 CARES filing deadline (~$11M DPS vs. $5.48M county). Natalie Beyer, Bettina Umstead, and BOCC Commissioners Wendy Jacobs and Heidi Carter pushed to form a joint city-county-DPS digital equity group, while Dr. Mubenga stressed DPS could not wait past June 1 to order student devices.

agenda_items.title: COVID-19 Updates and County Services Impact on DPS Families
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Dr. Nakia Hardy briefly summarized DPS's Reentry Planning Task Force, three-phase instructional packet distribution, and specialty high school graduations. County General Manager Joanne Pierce and BOCC Vice Chair Jacobs detailed essential DSS, immunization, and digital library services, while Xavier Cason and Natalie Beyer urged expanding mental-health resilience and summer youth programming alongside Spanish-language outreach.

agenda_items.title: Durham County FY 2020-21 Budget Overview and Face-Covering Project Update
agenda_items.discussion_summary: County Budget Director Keith Lane presented the FY21 recommended budget adding $5.23M for DPS ($3.2M operating, $2M capital; $151.2M direct plus $32M indirect/debt), prompting Natalie Beyer, Minnie Forte-Brown, and Dr. Mike Lee to highlight DPS's ~$15M shortfall for $15/hour wages and question county fund-balance comparisons ($62.46M unassigned / $211.1M total vs. DPS's $8.3M-$11M). Finally, BOCC Vice Chair Jacobs reported Duke physicists were evaluating masks for the joint face-covering project, backed by $40,000 from Durham and $10,000 from DPS travel funds.

votes.item_title: Approval of May 19, 2020 Joint BOE/BOCC Meeting Agenda
votes.notes: Joint meeting with the Durham Board of County Commissioners; reflects the seven DPS board members voting Aye alongside participating County Commissioners.
votes.discussion_detail: A member moved and another seconded approving the joint meeting agenda (with Chair Dr. Mike Lee noting a face-covering update could be fit in if time allowed). Passed unanimously on the joint BOE/BOCC roll call.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham Joint Board of County Commissioners and Board of Education Quarterly Meeting
disagreements.issue: FY21 County Budget Gap for DPS ($5.23M vs. $19M Request), Fund Balance Comparisons, and 2020 School Bond
disagreements.summary: DPS board members pressed county officials over the ~$15 million operating shortfall leaving $15/hour staff pay unfunded and resisted county comparisons of fund balances, while a proposal for a November 2020 bond drew county pushback.
disagreements.side_a_position: Seek deeper county operating/capital support—including exploring a modest November 2020 bond—and clarify that DPS's ~$8.3M-$11M fund balance is not comparable to the county's $62.5M unassigned ($211.1M total) reserves.
side_a_arguments: DPS's unanimous $19M request included $15/hour minimum wages for lowest-paid staff and level-funding needs (~$7M just to stay level), leaving a $15M gap.
Waiting until 2022 delays shovel-ready school projects, and DPS's small fund balance is already strained by COVID-19 expenses without net savings.
disagreements.side_b_position: Hold the FY21 increase at $5.23M ($3.2M operating, $2M capital) plus $176M in front-loaded LOBs while deferring any GO bond referendum to 2022.
side_b_arguments: A November 2020 bond would trigger an immediate property tax hike during a severe pandemic downturn, while LOBs already fund Northern High School and Elementary C.
The county carries $26M/year in existing school debt service and must preserve reserves to protect its AAA bond rating amid plunging sales taxes.
disagreements.resolution: No formal vote was taken; county staff provided the FY19 unassigned fund balance figure ($62,456,569) while both boards acknowledged continuing budget uncertainty from the General Assembly.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham Joint Board of County Commissioners and Board of Education Quarterly Meeting
disagreements.issue: Urgency of Joint City-County-DPS CARES Act Digital Equity Plan vs. Immediate Device Ordering
disagreements.summary: Board members and county commissioners debated whether the city, county, and DPS could quickly convene a joint task force to coordinate CARES Act funds for hotspots and devices before the June 1 filing deadline.
disagreements.side_a_position: Rapidly convene city, county, and school finance/leadership staff to align CARES Act funding on student digital access and countywide broadband.
side_a_arguments: Providing hotspots and fiber access addresses both immediate remote learning gaps and long-term rural/low-income equity across Durham.
disagreements.side_b_position: DPS cannot delay ordering devices past June 1 to wait on intergovernmental CARES negotiations, and the county's $5.48M CARES allocation faces competing small-business, food, and housing emergencies.
side_b_arguments: Global Chromebook demand requires a 60-day lead time starting before June 1, forcing DPS to front costs from fund balance first.
Durham County received only $5.48M in CARES funds compared to $11M for DPS and $194M for Wake County.
disagreements.resolution: Both boards expressed support for ongoing digital-equity collaboration between managers and Digital Durham while DPS proceeded immediately with its May 28 device procurement.
